arguments.issue: Did the Officer unreasonably reject the new evidence under paragraph 113(a) of IRPA?
arguments.claim: The Officer unreasonably rejected new evidence by not engaging with its credibility, relevance, and newness.
arguments.quote: The Officer’s concern was authentication. But the Officer did not say what further proof was needed, and did not engage with the Applicant’s affidavit.

support.ref: Raza v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385
Applicant’s affidavit, arrest warrant, news reports

arguments.weak_spot: The other side may argue the Officer reasonably doubted the authenticity of the documents.

arguments.issue: Did the Officer breach procedural fairness by making credibility findings without a hearing, contrary to paragraph 113(b) of IRPA and section 167 of the IRPR?
arguments.claim: The Officer made a credibility finding without a hearing, contrary to the prescribed factors.
arguments.quote: The Officer here said the warrant “could not be authenticated”, which is, in substance, a finding that the Applicant is not credible. All three of the section 167 factors are met.

support.ref: Singh v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FCA 96

arguments.weak_spot: The other side may argue the Officer did not make an explicit credibility finding or that a hearing was not required.

arguments.issue: Did the Officer apply the correct legal tests under sections 96 and 97 of IRPA?
arguments.claim: The Officer failed to separately assess the section 96 and 97 tests and focused only on credibility.
arguments.quote: The Officer did not assess either test separately and treated the question as one of credibility.

support.ref: Adjei v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1989] 2 FC 680 (CA)
Li v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FCA 1

arguments.weak_spot: The other side may argue the Officer’s reasons were sufficient and implicitly addressed the legal tests.
